claim: Voluntary reaction time typically becomes shorter when a delay period separates an instruction from a go cue.
source: Most fundamentally, the voluntary reaction time (RT) typically becomes shorter when a delay period separates an instruction from a go cue, presumably because the delay allows preparation time to complete (Rosenbaum, 1980; Riehle and Requin, 1993; Michaels et al., 2015; Churchland et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating this behavioral phenomenon.

claim: Neurons in primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) respond selectively during the delay period.
source: Neurons in many brain areas — including primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) — respond selectively during the delay (Tanji and Evarts, 1976; Riehle and Requin, 1993; Weinrich et al., 1984; Godschalk et al., 1985; Wise and Kurata, 1989; Kurata, 1989; Crammond and Kalaska, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies that have observed this neural activity pattern.

claim: Delay-period activity is predictive of reaction time variability.
source: In support of this interpretation, delay-period activity is predictive of RT variability (Riehle and Requin, 1993; Michaels et al., 2015; Bastian et al., 2003; Churchland et al., 2006; Afshar et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies that have demonstrated this relationship.

claim: Disruption of delay-period activity erases reaction time savings provided by the delay.
source: and its disruption erases RT-savings provided by the delay (Churchland and Shenoy, 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study that performed this causal manipulation.

claim: Delay-period activity and movement-related activity occupy orthogonal population-level subspaces.
source: To overcome this challenge, we leveraged the recent finding (Elsayed et al., 2016) that delay-period activity and movement-related activity occupy orthogonal population-level subspaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study that made this discovery.

claim: Putatively preparatory events were conserved across all contexts (cue-initiated, self-initiated, and quasi-automatic).
source: Putatively preparatory events were conserved across all contexts.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: An appropriate preparatory state is consistently achieved before movement onset.
source: Our findings support the hypothesis that an appropriate preparatory state is consistently achieved before movement onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: The preparatory process can consume surprisingly little time.
source: However, our results reveal that this process can consume surprisingly little time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, particularly from the quasi-automatic context.

claim: Two monkeys (Ba and Ax) were trained to execute reaches from a central touch-point to radially arranged targets.
source: We trained two monkeys (Ba and Ax) to execute reaches from a central touch-point to radially arranged targets.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and subjects used in the study.

claim: In the cue-initiated context, a variable delay period (0–1000 ms) separated target onset from an explicit go cue.
source: The cue-initiated context (Figure 1a) emulated the standard instructed-delay paradigm: a variable delay period (0–1000 ms) separated target onset from an explicit go cue.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the cue-initiated context, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: In the self-initiated context, monkeys were free to reach upon target onset but received larger rewards if they chose to wait.
source: We also employed a 'self-initiated' context: monkeys were free to reach upon target onset but received larger rewards if they chose to wait.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the self-initiated context.

claim: The quasi-automatic context used moving targets to evoke particularly low-latency reaches.
source: To examine preparation without a delay, we did not simply reduce the cue-initiated delay to zero (as in Crammond and Kalaska, 2000; Churchland et al., 2006; Ames et al., 2014) but instead adopted the paradigm of (Perfiliev et al., 2010) and used moving targets. Because moving targets evoke particularly low-latency reaches, this 'quasi-automatic' context provides a stringent test of the prediction that delay-period-like activity should appear in the absence of a delay.
evidence: This describes the rationale and design of the quasi-automatic context.

claim: Cue-initiated reaction times were 253 ± 50 ms for monkey Ba and 235 ± 37 ms for monkey Ax.
source: Cue-initiated RTs were 253 ± 50 ms and 235 ± 37 ms (mean ±standard deviation) for monkey Ba and Ax (Figure 2a,b, red traces).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of reaction times from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Self-initiated reaction times were 935 ms ± 132 ms for monkey Ba and 996 ms ± 106 ms for monkey Ax.
source: Self-initiated RTs were 935 ms ± 132 ms and 996 ms ± 106 ms for the two monkeys (Figure 2a,b, blue).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of reaction times from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Quasi-automatic reaction times were 205 ± 32 ms for monkey Ba and 192 ms ± 27 ms for monkey Ax.
source: Quasi-automatic RTs were 205 ± 32 ms and 192 ms ± 27 ms for monkey Ba and Ax (Figure 2a,b, yellow).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of reaction times from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Quasi-automatic reaction times were shorter than cue-initiated reaction times by 48 ms and 43 ms on average.
source: Despite the lack of time to prepare in advance, quasi-automatic RTs were shorter than cue-initiated RTs: by 48 and 43 ms on average.
evidence: This is a comparison of reaction times calculated from the experimental data.

claim: The earliest onset of EMG in the quasi-automatic context occurred around 100 ms after target onset based on trial-averaged rectified EMG.
source: First, for all muscles, we computed trial-averaged rectified EMG, time-locked to target onset (Figure 3, one colored trace per condition). The earliest change typically occurred around 100 ms.
evidence: This is a measurement from the EMG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Single-trial EMG onset could be as early as 90 ms after the go cue for monkey Ba and 110 ms for monkey Ax in the quasi-automatic context.
source: EMG onset could be rapid: as early as 90 ms after the go cue for monkey Ba (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and 110 ms for monkey A (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from single-trial EMG data shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: Low-latency EMG responses in the quasi-automatic context are consistent with the earliest onset of EMG in Perfiliev et al. (2010): 90–110 ms across subjects.
source: These low latencies are consistent with the earliest onset of EMG in (Perfiliev et al., 2010): 90–110 ms across subjects.
evidence: This compares the current findings with prior published results.

claim: Reach kinematics were well-matched across contexts with only small differences.
source: The match in kinematics was indeed quite good (Figure 2c–h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with only small differences across contexts.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinematic data shown in Figure 2c-h and supplement.

claim: Quasi-automatic reaches had slightly greater extent and slightly higher peak velocity (on average 7% and 9% higher relative to cue-initiated movements).
source: Quasi-automatic reaches tended to have a slightly greater extent and a slightly higher peak velocity (on average 7% and 9% higher relative to cue-initiated movements) but were otherwise very similar to cue-initiated and self-initiated reaches.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of kinematic measurements across contexts.

claim: Quasi-automatic reaches were consistently target directed even for the earliest reaches.
source: This was not the case: even the earliest reaches were consistently target directed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) as in (Perfiliev et al., 2010), and hand trajectories did not exhibit guesses with subsequent corrections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinematic data shown in Figure 2 supplements, consistent with prior work.

claim: Quasi-automatic movements were slightly less accurate than cue-initiated movements: the circular standard deviation of initial reach direction was 17% and 11% higher for monkey Ba and Ax (p<0.001 for both).
source: Yet while quasi-automatic movements were consistently target-directed, they were slightly less accurate: the circular standard deviation (Berens, 2009) of initial reach direction was 17% and 11% higher (monkey Ba and Ax; p<0.001 for both).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of reach accuracy across contexts.

claim: Muscle activity patterns were very similar across contexts during movement.
source: EMG response patterns were very similar across contexts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). During movement, the median correlation between the self-initiated and cue-initiated contexts was 0.98 and 0.98 (monkey Ba and Ax respectively; activity compared in a 300 ms window starting 50 ms before movement onset; median taken across muscles). The median correlation between quasi-automatic and cue-initiated contexts was 0.97 and 0.96.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of EMG patterns shown in Figure 3 supplement.

claim: There was little change in baseline EMG during the delay period in the cue-initiated and self-initiated contexts.
source: As desired, there was little change in baseline EMG during that interval (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). For the cue-initiated context, the across-condition variance of EMG (i.e. selectivity for direction) during the delay was 0.76% and 2.8% of the variance during movement. For the self-initiated context, corresponding values were 0.51% and 1.2% (measured during the interval from target onset until 250 ms before movement onset).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of EMG variance during different epochs.

claim: Spikes of well-isolated neurons were recorded from the arm region of motor cortex, including M1 and the immediately adjacent region of PMd (129 and 172 neurons for monkey Ba and Ax).
source: Spikes of well-isolated neurons were recorded from the arm region of motor cortex, including M1 and the immediately adjacent region of PMd (129 and 172 neurons for monkey Ba and Ax).
evidence: This describes the neural recording methodology and sample size.

claim: Delay-epoch activity varied significantly with reach direction (ANOVA, p<0.05) for 74/129 neurons in monkey Ba and 88/172 neurons in monkey Ax.
source: Delay-epoch activity varied significantly with reach direction (ANOVA, p<0.05) for the majority of neurons (74/129 and 88/172 for monkey Ba and Ax).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of neural selectivity during the delay epoch.

claim: Movement-epoch activity varied significantly with target direction for 116/129 neurons in monkey Ba and 144/172 neurons in monkey Ax.
source: Movement-epoch activity also varied significantly with target direction for most neurons (116/129 and 144/172).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of neural selectivity during the movement epoch.

claim: In the self-initiated context, pre-movement activity grew stronger with time and came to resemble delay-period activity in the cue-initiated context.
source: Single-neuron responses followed the second prediction. Pre-movement activity in the self-initiated context grew stronger with time and came to resemble delay-period activity in the cue-initiated context.
evidence: This is an observation from the neural data comparing activity patterns across contexts.

claim: During the first 150 ms after target onset in the self-initiated context, the median correlation between self-initiated and cue-initiated activity patterns was low (across-neuron median r = 0.39 and 0.16 for the two monkeys).
source: During the first 150 ms after target onset, the median correlation between self-initiated and cue-initiated activity patterns was low (across-neuron median r = 0.39 and 0.16 for the two monkeys), largely because activity was often weak in the self-initiated context.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neural activity patterns across contexts.

claim: In the self-initiated context, correlations between self-initiated and cue-initiated activity patterns became stronger as movement onset neared (median r = 0.86 and 0.74, using a 150 ms window ending 50 ms before movement onset).
source: Correlations became stronger as movement onset neared (median r = 0.86 and 0.74, using a 150 ms window ending 50 ms before movement onset).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neural activity patterns across contexts at different time points.

claim: During movement in the self-initiated context, the correlation between self-initiated and cue-initiated activity was quite high (median r = 0.92 and 0.87).
source: During movement, the correlation was quite high (median r = 0.92 and 0.87).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neural activity patterns during movement across contexts.

claim: Movement-related responses in the quasi-automatic context closely resembled those in the other two contexts.
source: Movement-related responses in the quasi-automatic context closely resembled those in the other two contexts (compare across rows in Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the neural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The median correlation between quasi-automatic and cue-initiated movement-epoch activity patterns was 0.85 and 0.85 for monkey Ba and Ax.
source: The median correlation between quasi-automatic and cue-initiated movement-epoch activity patterns was 0.85 and 0.85 (monkey Ba and Ax).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neural activity patterns during movement across contexts.

claim: Twelve preparatory dimensions captured 80% of delay-epoch firing rate variance but only 3% of movement-epoch variance for monkey Ba.
source: We identified twelve dimensions, collectively the putative 'preparatory subspace', that captured 80% of delay-epoch firing rate variance but only 3% of movement-epoch variance.
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality reduction analysis applied to the neural data.

claim: Twelve movement dimensions captured 85% of movement-epoch variance but only 3% of delay-epoch variance for monkey Ba.
source: We isolated twelve further dimensions, collectively the 'movement subspace', that captured 85% of movement-epoch variance but only 3% of delay-epoch variance.
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality reduction analysis applied to the neural data.

claim: For monkey Ax, preparatory dimensions captured 72% of delay-epoch variance versus 4% of movement-epoch variance, and movement dimensions captured 83% of movement-epoch variance versus 3% of delay-epoch variance.
source: The above percentages are for monkey Ba and were similar for monkey Ax (72% versus 4% and 83% versus 3%).
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality reduction analysis applied to the neural data for monkey Ax.

claim: The response of neuron 88 was accurately reconstructed (R2 = 0.93) as the sum of a preparatory-subspace pattern and a movement-subspace pattern.
source: For example, the response of neuron 88 (Figure 6, rightmost column) is accurately approximated as the sum of a preparatory-subspace pattern (a weighted sum of preparatory projections, orange) and a movement-subspace pattern (a weighted sum of movement projections, purple). The reconstruction is quite good (R2 = 0.93, compare with Figure 5a, top), reflecting the high proportion of variance captured in the two subspaces.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of reconstruction accuracy shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the self-initiated context, the total variance captured across the two subspaces was 89% (monkey Ba) and 84% (monkey Ax) of that in the cue-initiated context.
source: In the self-initiated context, the total variance captured across the two subspaces was 89% (monkey Ba) and 84% (monkey Ax) of that in the cue-initiated context.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of variance captured across contexts.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, the total variance captured across the two subspaces was 87% and 84% of that in the cue-initiated context for monkey Ba and Ax.
source: In the quasi-automatic context, the total variance captured was 87% and 84% of that in the cue-initiated context.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of variance captured across contexts.

claim: Preparatory-subspace patterns exhibit similar tuning across contexts, with regression slopes strongly positive when comparing self-initiated and quasi-automatic contexts against cue-initiated context.
source: Slopes were strongly positive (Figure 7c,d, black bars) indicating that preparatory-subspace activity varies with reach direction in a similar way for all contexts.
evidence: This is a result from the regression analysis shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: Movement-subspace occupancy exhibited a similar time-course for all three contexts: occupancy was negligible until ~100 ms before movement onset and peaked just after movement onset.
source: Movement-subspace occupancy exhibited a similar time-course for all three contexts (Figure 8, purple traces): occupancy was negligible until ~100 ms before movement onset and peaked just after movement onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the occupancy analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the cue-initiated context, preparatory-subspace occupancy rose sharply following target onset and was sustained at a lower level throughout the delay.
source: In the cue-initiated context, occupancy rose sharply following target onset and was sustained at a lower level throughout the delay (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is an observation from the occupancy analysis shown in Figure 8a.

claim: In the cue-initiated context, preparatory-subspace occupancy declined rapidly just before movement onset, reaching near-baseline levels around the time movement began.
source: Occupancy declined rapidly just before movement onset, reaching near-baseline levels around the time movement began (flanking traces show SEMs; see Table 2 for key p-values).
evidence: This is an observation from the occupancy analysis shown in Figure 8a, with statistical support in Table 2.

claim: In the self-initiated context, the post-target peak in preparatory-subspace occupancy was significantly weaker than for the cue-initiated context.
source: In the self-initiated context, preparatory-subspace occupancy developed more sluggishly (Figure 8b). The post-target peak was significantly weaker than for the cue-initiated context.
evidence: This is an observation from the occupancy analysis shown in Figure 8b, with statistical support indicated.

claim: In the self-initiated context, preparatory-subspace occupancy grew as movement approached, reaching a peak shortly before movement onset.
source: Preparatory-subspace occupancy then grew as movement approached, reaching a peak shortly before movement onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the occupancy analysis shown in Figure 8b.

claim: By 150 ms before movement onset in the self-initiated context, preparatory-subspace occupancy was similar for the self-initiated and cue-initiated contexts: slightly greater for monkey Ba (p<0.003) and slightly smaller for monkey Ax (N.S.).
source: By 150 ms before movement onset, preparatory-subspace occupancy was similar for the self-initiated and cue-initiated contexts: slightly greater for monkey Ba (p<0.003) and slightly smaller for monkey Ax (N.S.).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of occupancy values across contexts.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, preparatory-subspace occupancy rose rapidly following target onset and peaked shortly before movement onset.
source: In the quasi-automatic context, preparatory-subspace occupancy rose rapidly following target onset and peaked shortly before movement onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the occupancy analysis shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Peak preparatory-subspace occupancy in the quasi-automatic context was slightly but significantly greater than the pre-movement peak in the other two contexts (p<0.002 for all comparisons).
source: Peak occupancy was slightly but significantly greater than the pre-movement peak in the other two contexts (p<0.002 for all comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of peak occupancy values across contexts.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, preparatory-subspace occupancy precedes movement-subspace occupancy by 33 ms for monkey Ba and 42 ms for monkey Ax (assessed using a threshold of 10% of the peak, p<0.001 for both).
source: However, that putatively preparatory stage appears to be very rapid: preparatory-subspace occupancy precedes movement-subspace occupancy by only a few tens of milliseconds: 33 ms for monkey Ba and 42 ms for monkey Ax (assessed using a threshold of 10% of the peak, p<0.001 for both).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the temporal relationship between preparatory and movement subspace occupancy.

claim: For short-RT quasi-automatic trials, preparatory-subspace occupancy continued to show a pre-movement surge.
source: For the quasi-automatic context (yellow traces) short-RT trials continued to show a pre-movement surge in preparatory-subspace occupancy. Indeed, the pre-movement peak was actually slightly higher for short-RT quasi-automatic trials versus short-RT cue-initiated trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of short-RT trials shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Across all contexts, preparatory-subspace activity always emerged before movement-subspace activity began.
source: Across all contexts, preparatory-subspace activity always emerged before movement-subspace activity began.
evidence: This is a general observation from the state-space analyses shown in Figure 10.

claim: Preparatory-subspace activity and movement-subspace activity overlapped temporally: the former declined as the latter emerged.
source: Preparatory-subspace activity and movement-subspace activity overlapped temporally: the former declined as the latter emerged.
evidence: This is an observation from the state-space analyses shown in Figure 10.

claim: Just before and during the overlap between preparatory and movement subspace activity, the pattern of preparatory-subspace activity was similar across contexts.
source: Just before and during that overlap, the pattern of preparatory-subspace activity was similar across contexts.
evidence: This is an observation from the state-space analyses shown in Figure 10.

claim: Movement-subspace patterns were highly correlated across contexts, with correlations ranging from 0.94 to 0.99 for monkey Ba and from 0.88 to 0.99 for monkey Ax (p<0.0001 in all cases).
source: Correlations were high for all comparisons. Comparing self-initiated and cue-initiated contexts, correlations for the two dimensions shown in Figure 10 were 0.96 ± 0.01 (95% CI) and 0.98 ± 0.01 for monkey Ba, and 0.98 ± 0.01 and 0.97 ± 0.01 for monkey Ax. Across the twelve movement dimensions, correlations ranged from 0.94 to 0.99 for monkey Ba and from 0.91 to 0.99 for monkey Ax (p<0.0001 in all cases). Correlations were similarly high when comparing quasi-automatic and cue-initiated contexts. For the two dimensions shown in Figure 10, correlations were 0.96 ± 0.02 and 0.98 ± 0.01 for monkey Ba, and 0.95 ± 0.02 and 0.96 ± 0.02 for monkey Ax. Across all movement dimensions, correlations ranged from 0.94 to 0.98 for monkey Ba and from 0.88 to 0.98 for monkey Ax (p<0.0001 in all cases).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of movement-subspace patterns across contexts.

claim: The final preparatory state (55 ms before movement onset) was similar across contexts, with correlations between contexts ranging from 0.91 to 0.99 (all p<0.001).
source: The final preparatory state was similar across contexts. For each reach direction, the triplet of neural states for the three contexts formed a cluster (grouped via covariance ellipses in Figure 11a,b). Clusters were quite tight for monkey Ba and somewhat less so for monkey Ax. To quantify tightness of clustering – i.e. the similarity of states across contexts – we computed the correlation, between contexts, of the set of preparatory-subspace states (one state per reach direction). Considering the top two dimensions, the correlation between cue-initiated and self-initiated contexts was 0.99 for monkey Ba and 0.95 for monkey Ax (95% CIs were 0.98–0.99 and 0.86–0.98). The correlation between cue-initiated and quasi-automatic contexts was 0.99 for monkey Ba and 0.91 for monkey Ax (0.97–1.0 and 0.76–0.97). The correlation between self-initiated and quasi-automatic contexts was 0.99 for monkey Ba and 0.92 for monkey Ax (0.97–1.0 and 0.79–0.97). All correlations were statistically significant (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of preparatory states across contexts, shown in Figure 11a,b.

claim: When comparing the self-initiated and cue-initiated contexts, covariance between preparatory states peaked slightly more than 100 ms before movement onset for both monkeys.
source: When comparing the self-initiated and cue-initiated contexts (Figure 11c,d; blue) covariance rose as movement approached, peaking slightly more than 100 ms (monkey Ba and Ax) before movement onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the covariance analysis shown in Figure 11c,d.

claim: When comparing the quasi-automatic and cue-initiated contexts, covariance between preparatory states peaked ~65 ms and ~75 ms (monkey Ba and Ax) before movement onset.
source: When comparing the quasi-automatic and cue-initiated contexts (Figure 11c,d; yellow) covariance rose rapidly, peaking ~65 ms and ~75 ms (monkey Ba and Ax) before movement onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the covariance analysis shown in Figure 11c,d.

claim: Movement-subspace activity began ~75 ms (monkey Ba) and ~80 ms (monkey Ax) prior to movement onset in the quasi-automatic context.
source: These peaks occur just after activity in the movement-subspace first begins to change, at ~75 ms (monkey Ba) and ~80 ms (monkey Ax) prior to movement onset in the quasi-automatic context.
evidence: This is a measurement of the timing of movement-subspace activity onset.

claim: The movement subspace became occupied just before the onset of changes in EMG, with an average latency of 21 ms across monkeys and contexts.
source: Across monkeys and contexts, the movement subspace always became occupied just before the onset of changes in EMG, with an average latency of 21 ms.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neural and EMG timing.

claim: The latency between the onset of movement-subspace activity and muscle activity was 27 and 20 ms (cue-initiated), 33 and 22 ms (self-initiated), and 19 and 6 ms (quasi-automatic) for monkey Ba and Ax.
source: The latency between the onset of movement-subspace activity and muscle activity was, for monkey Ba and Ax, 27 and 20 ms (cue-initiated), 33 and 22 ms (self-initiated) and 19 and 6 ms (quasi-automatic).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the temporal relationship between neural and muscle activity across contexts.

claim: Delay-period and movement-related selectivity typically differ when a greater range of movements is used.
source: Later experiments leveraged a greater range of movements, revealing that delay-period and movement-related selectivity typically differ (Crammond and Kalaska, 2000; Elsayed et al., 2016; Churchland et al., 2010; Kaufman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies that have demonstrated this finding.

claim: It has been suggested that delay-period activity may initialize neural dynamics that will produce movement.
source: It was instead suggested that delay-period activity may initialize neural dynamics that will produce movement (Churchland et al., 2006; Churchland et al., 2010; Churchland et al., 2012; Churchland and Cunningham, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies that have proposed this hypothesis.

claim: A recent study yielded mixed evidence for the hypothesis that delay-period activity initializes movement-generating dynamics when comparing activity with and without a delay.
source: Yet a recent study yielded mixed evidence for this hypothesis when comparing activity with and without a delay (Ames et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The present results reveal that the neural process present during a delay-period is not specific to that situation.
source: The present results reveal that the neural process present during a delay-period is not specific to that situation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Rising preparatory-subspace occupancy in the self-initiated context is consistent with the hypothesis that preparatory-subspace activity is preparatory rather than suppressive.
source: The rise in preparatory subspace occupancy as movement approaches is consistent with the hypothesis that preparatory-subspace activity is preparatory. Were it suppressive, activity should wane as movement becomes more probable.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed pattern of preparatory-subspace occupancy in the self-initiated context.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, EMG latencies could be as short as 90–110 ms on some trials, indicating there cannot exist an obligatory preparatory process that necessarily takes 100–200 ms to complete.
source: In the quasi-automatic context, EMG latencies could be as short as 90–110 ms on some trials. Thus, there cannot exist an obligatory preparatory process that necessarily takes 100–200 ms to complete.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the EMG latency measurements.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, preparatory subspace activity leads movement-subspace activity by only ~40 ms, and the preparatory-subspace state came to match that in the cue-initiated context in ~70 ms.
source: Neural data are consistent with a preparatory process that can be very rapid. In the quasi-automatic context, preparatory subspace activity leads movement-subspace activity by only ~40 ms, and the preparatory-subspace state came to match that in the cue-initiated context in ~70 ms.
evidence: This is a summary of timing measurements from the neural data.

claim: These findings rule out the idea of a slow, cognitive planning process that must complete before movement begins.
source: These findings rule out the idea of a slow, cognitive planning process that must complete before movement begins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rapid timing of preparatory events observed in the data.

claim: The ability to rapidly and consistently achieve the correct preparatory state may be uncertain in many real-world situations, leading the motor system to prepare in advance when possible.
source: We can only speculate, but the ability to rapidly and consistently achieve the correct preparatory state may be uncertain in many real-world situations. The motor system may thus have developed the strategy of preparing in advance when possible, allowing time to correct small inaccuracies before movement begins (Churchland et al., 2006; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007a).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why preparation occurs in advance when time is available, supported by citations.

claim: Rapid preparation may be feasible only for well-practiced movements, leading to a default strategy of preparing in advance when possible.
source: More broadly, rapid preparation may be feasible only for well-practiced movements, leading to a default strategy of preparing in advance when possible.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the conditions under which rapid preparation is possible.

claim: The overlap between preparatory and movement subspace activity is consistent with (and required by) the hypothesis that preparatory-subspace activity seeds movement-subspace dynamics.
source: This overlap is consistent with (and indeed required by) the hypothesis that preparatory-subspace activity seeds movement-subspace dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional relationship between preparatory and movement activity.

claim: The present results support and extend the conclusion of Ames et al. that the initial response to target onset is similar for zero-delay and long-delay trials.
source: With this conflict resolved, the present results support and extend two key conclusions of Ames et al. First, the initial response to target onset is similar for zero-delay and long-delay trials (Figure 10a, compare the 'target' panel between cue-initiated and quasi-automatic contexts).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work, supported by the data shown in Figure 10a.

claim: When under time pressure, the neural state does not momentarily pause at a stable state prior to the onset of movement-related activity.
source: Second, when under time pressure, the neural state does not momentarily pause at a stable state prior to the onset of movement-related activity (also see (Michaels et al., 2015)).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, consistent with prior work.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, events are so compressed that preparatory-subspace activity is still developing as movement-subspace activity is beginning.
source: Indeed, in the quasi-automatic context, events are so compressed that preparatory-subspace activity is still developing as movement-subspace activity is beginning.
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal dynamics of neural activity in the quasi-automatic context.

claim: Network models produce preparatory activity that is relatively stable during the delay but is not perfectly static.
source: More sophisticated network models (Sussillo et al., 2015; Michaels et al., 2016) produce similar but less-idealized responses: preparatory activity is relatively stable during the delay but is not perfectly static.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to network modeling studies.

claim: The empirical population response during the cue-initiated context behaved much like that of network models, with activity developing quickly and remaining relatively stable across the delay but with some fluctuations.
source: The empirical population response during the cue-initiated context behaved much like that of network models. In the dominant preparatory dimensions, activity developed quickly and remained relatively stable across the delay. However, there were still some fluctuations with time, as can be seen in both state-space plots (Figure 10) and in projections as a function of time (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a comparison between the observed data and network model predictions.

claim: Very unstable activity during a memory period was recently observed in parietal cortex and ventral premotor cortex.
source: Very unstable activity during a memory period was recently observed in parietal cortex and ventral premotor cortex (Michaels et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The stability of preparatory activity may be area-specific, being more stable in areas where it serves a direct pre-motor purpose.
source: However, a more interesting possibility is that the stability of preparatory activity may be area-specific. Activity may be more stable in areas where it serves a direct pre-motor purpose (initializing movement-period dynamics) and less so in areas where it relates to anticipation or more cognitive aspects of the task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of differences in preparatory activity stability across brain areas.

claim: Pre-movement activity in a variety of brain regions can reflect decisions regarding when or where to move.
source: It is well established that pre-movement activity in a variety of brain regions can reflect decisions regarding when or where to move (Thura et al., 2012; Cisek and Kalaska, 2005; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Kaufman et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Rising preparatory-subspace activity in the self-initiated context presumably reflects preparation to execute a choice that was clear from the outset.
source: However, in the present study, the target was always fully specified; target choice did not become more certain with time. Thus, rising preparatory-subspace activity presumably reflects preparation to execute a choice that was clear from the outset (also see (Murakami et al., 2014; Schurger et al., 2012)).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rising preparatory activity in the self-initiated context, supported by citations.

claim: There exist at least three separable pre-movement processes: deciding what to do, preparing to do it, and initiating movement.
source: Our interpretation is that there exist at least three separable pre-movement processes: deciding what to do, preparing to do it, and initiating movement.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the different processes involved in movement generation.

claim: These three pre-movement processes occur with variable timing relative to one another, occurring very close in time (all within 100 ms) for the quasi-automatic context but staggered for the self-initiated context.
source: It appears these processes occur with variable timing relative to one another. They occur very close in time (all within 100 ms) for the quasi-automatic context but are staggered for the self-initiated context.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of neural events across different contexts.

claim: Preparatory-subspace activity develops hundreds of milliseconds before movement onset in the self-initiated context, presumably before a definitive choice to trigger movement has been made.
source: In particular, preparatory-subspace activity develops hundreds of milliseconds before movement onset in the self-initiated context, presumably before a definitive choice to trigger movement has been made.
evidence: This is an observation from the timing of preparatory activity in the self-initiated context.

claim: Similar movements may be preceded and accompanied by divergent neural events depending on how and why a movement is prepared and initiated.
source: It seems a near-certainty that similar movements may be preceded and accompanied by divergent neural events depending on how and why a movement is prepared and initiated.
evidence: This is a general statement about context-dependent neural activity, supported by knowledge of neural variability.

claim: A prepared movement can be triggered involuntarily by the subcortically mediated startle reflex.
source: As one example, while a prepared movement can be initiated in response to a learned visual cue, it can also be triggered involuntarily by the subcortically mediated startle reflex (Valls-Solé et al., 1995; Carlsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The three contexts studied evoke quite different movement-epoch responses in the supplementary motor area.
source: As another example, the three contexts studied here evoke quite different movement-epoch responses in the supplementary motor area (Lara et al., 2018), despite the similarity of the movements themselves.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to another study.

claim: Motor cortex plays a more consistent role across contexts, with similar movements driven by similar patterns of movement-related activity, preceded by similar patterns of preparatory activity.
source: Yet the present results reveal that motor cortex plays a more consistent role across contexts. While context impacted the timing of neural events, in the end, similar movements were driven by similar patterns of movement-related activity, preceded by similar patterns of preparatory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data comparing neural activity across contexts.

claim: Subjects were two adult male macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) aged 10 and 14 years and weighing 11–13 Kg.
source: Subjects were two adult male macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) aged 10 and 14 years and weighing 11–13 Kg at the time of the experiments.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: All procedures were in accord with the US National Institutes of Health guidelines and were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (AC-AAAQ7409).
source: All procedures were in accord with the US National Institutes of Health guidelines and were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (AC-AAAQ7409).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Hand position was monitored using an infrared optical system (Polaris; Northern Digital) to track (~0.3 mm precision) a reflective bead temporarily affixed to the third and fourth digits.
source: Hand position was monitored using an infrared optical system (Polaris; Northern Digital) to track (~0.3 mm precision) a reflective bead temporarily affixed to the third and fourth digits.
evidence: This describes the method used to track hand position.

claim: Target distance was 130 mm for cue and self-initiated contexts and 40 mm for the quasi-automatic context.
source: Target distance was 130 mm for cue and self-initiated contexts and 40 mm for the quasi-automatic context (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters for target distance.

claim: In the cue-initiated context, reaches were successful if they were initiated within 500 ms of the go cue, had a duration <500 ms, and landed within an 18 mm radius window centered on the target.
source: Reaches were successful if they were initiated within 500 ms of the go cue, had a duration <500 ms, and landed within an 18 mm radius window centered on the target.
evidence: This describes the success criteria for the cue-initiated context.

claim: In the self-initiated context, the reward for a correct reach grew exponentially starting at 1 drop and achieved a maximum of 8 drops after 1200 ms.
source: The reward for a correct reach grew exponentially starting at 1 drop and achieved a maximum of 8 drops after 1200 ms.
evidence: This describes the reward structure for the self-initiated context.

claim: In the quasi-automatic context, target speed and initial location were titrated during training such that the target was typically intercepted ~130 mm from the touch-point.
source: Target speed and initial location (40 mm from the touch-point) were titrated, during training, such that the target was typically intercepted ~130 mm from the touch-point (the same location as the targets for the other two contexts).
evidence: This describes how the quasi-automatic task parameters were calibrated.

claim: Monkeys successfully completed more than 90% of trials for every context.
source: This task was challenging, but monkeys successfully completed the majority of trials (>90% for every context and both monkeys).
evidence: This is a summary of task performance across contexts.

claim: A photodetector was used to synchronize commands from the behavioral control software with the 60 Hz refresh schedule of the display.
source: We used a photodetector (Thorlabs) to synchronize commands from the behavioral control software with the 60 Hz refresh schedule of the display.
evidence: This describes the method used to ensure precise timing of visual stimuli.

claim: Movement onset was estimated based on hand speed (the magnitude of velocity).
source: Movement onset was estimated based on hand speed: the magnitude of velocity.
evidence: This describes the method used to estimate movement onset.

claim: After subjects became proficient in the task, sterile surgery was performed to implant a head restraint and a recording chamber centered over the arm area of primary motor cortex (M1) and the dorsal premotor cortex (PMd).
source: After subjects became proficient in the task, we performed sterile surgery to implant a head restraint. At the same time, we implanted a recording chamber centered over the arm area of primary motor cortex (M1) and the dorsal premotor cortex (PMd.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedures used to enable neural recordings.

claim: Intra-cortical microstimulation was used to confirm that recordings were from the forelimb region of motor cortex.
source: We used intra-cortical microstimulation to confirm that our recordings were from the forelimb region of motor cortex (biphasic pulses, cathodal leading, 250µS pulse width delivered at 333 Hz for a total duration of 50 ms).
evidence: This describes the method used to verify recording location.

claim: Microstimulation typically evoked contractions of the shoulder and upper-arm muscles, at currents from 5 μA – 60 μA depending on location and stimulation depth.
source: Microstimulation typically evoked contractions of the shoulder and upper-arm muscles, at currents from 5 μA – 60 μA depending on location and stimulation depth.
evidence: This describes the results of microstimulation used to verify recording location.

claim: All well-isolated task-responsive neurons were recorded; no attempt was made to screen for neuronal selectivity for reach direction or any other response property.
source: We recorded all well-isolated task-responsive neurons; no attempt was made to screen for neuronal selectivity for reach direction or any other response property.
evidence: This describes the neuron selection criteria for recordings.

claim: Spikes were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation of 20 ms and averaged across trials to produce peri-stimulus time histograms.
source: Spikes were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation of 20 ms and averaged across trials to produce peri-stimulus time histograms.
evidence: This describes the method used to process neural spike data.

claim: EMG signals were bandpass filtered (10–500 Hz), digitized at 1 kHz, rectified, smoothed with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation of 20 ms, and averaged across trials.
source: EMG signals were bandpass filtered (10–500 Hz), digitized at 1 kHz, rectified, smoothed with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation of 20 ms, and averaged across trials to produce a continuous estimate of muscle activity intensity (very roughly analogous to a firing rate).
evidence: This describes the method used to process EMG data.

claim: For analyses of latency, a 10 ms Gaussian kernel was used rather than 20 ms to minimize the impact of filtering on the moment that activity first began to change.
source: For analyses of latency (Figure 3, and the comparison between the onset of movement-subspace activity and EMG) we used a 10 ms Gaussian kernel, rather than 20 ms. We did so to minimize the small impact of filtering on the moment that activity first began to change.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice for latency analyses.

claim: Two pre-processing steps were employed before applying dimensionality reduction: soft-normalization of neural responses and mean-centering at each time.
source: As in our previous work, we employed two pre-processing steps (Churchland et al., 2012) before applying dimensionality reduction. First, the responses of each neuron were soft-normalized so that neurons with high firing rates had approximately unity firing-rate range (normalization factor = firing rate range + 5). This step ensures that subsequent dimensionality reduction (see below) captures the response of all neurons, rather than a handful of high firing-rate neurons. Second, the responses for each neuron were mean-centered at each time as follows: we calculated the mean activity across all conditions of each neuron at each time point, and subtracted this mean activity from each condition's response. This step ensures that dimensionality reduction focuses on dimensions where responses are selective across conditions, rather than dimensions where activity varies in a similar fashion across all conditions (Kaufman et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the data pre-processing methods used before dimensionality reduction.

claim: The dimensionality reduction method specifically sought dimensions capturing response aspects that vary with condition (i.e. are 'tuned' for reach direction).
source: We specifically sought dimensions capturing response aspects that vary with condition (i.e. are 'tuned' for reach direction). Untuned response aspects exist in separate, largely orthogonal, dimensions (Kaufman et al., 2014) and are not analyzed here.
evidence: This describes what aspects of neural activity the method was designed to capture.

claim: A bootstrap procedure was used to estimate the sampling error of the subspace occupancy by creating 1000 surrogate populations by redrawing with replacement from the original population.
source: To estimate the sampling error of the subspace occupancy we used a bootstrap procedure. We created 1000 surrogate populations by redrawing with replacement from the original population. We computed the subspace occupancy for each surrogate population. This yields, for each time, a sampling distribution of the occupancy.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used to estimate uncertainty in occupancy measurements.

claim: For comparing timing of muscle activity with neural activity entering the movement subspace, spike trains were filtered using a Gaussian kernel with 10 ms standard deviation.
source: For the neural data, we filtered the spike trains of all neurons using a Gaussian kernel with 10 ms standard deviation (rather than 20 ms for all other analyses of neural data).
evidence: This describes the filtering method used for latency comparisons.

claim: Latency was measured as the first moment in time when occupancy or activity reached 10% of peak.
source: We measured the latency as the first moment in time when occupancy reached 10% of peak occupancy.
evidence: This describes the method used to measure latency.
